hypothesis.title: The Relation Matrix
hypothesis.question: When musical objects stay fixed, can changing only their relational matrix alter perceived dialogue, coherence, and arrival quality?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If the same six sound objects are rearranged by explicit relation matrices—call/answer distance, harmonic graph adjacency, nearest-accessible transition, token/envelope alignment, and invariant/adaptive surface mapping—then listeners will report stronger differences in dialogue, spatial coherence, and formal inevitability than in an object-only control, because the cited sources all show meaning or stability emerging from relations rather than isolated objects.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: S1 frames call-and-response as a structural relation operating from beats to whole arrangement sections, including silence as an answering element. S5 formalizes harmonic resources as graph/configuration relations rather than isolated chords, while S6 shows that sound-source positions can be recovered from Euclidean distance and TDOA relations. S3 adds that mismatched text/speech unit alignment destabilizes streaming speech prosody, and S4 separates relatively invariant encoder representations from decoder layers that adapt to degradation. S2 supplies the physical analogy: systems often move to the nearest accessible metastable state rather than the globally optimal one. Together these support a test in which fixed audio objects are made to feel different by changing the relation matrix among them [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6].

recipe.title: Relation-Matrix Variations
recipe.bodyMd: Create a 60-second loop from six fixed sound objects: a call phrase, answer phrase, bass riff, chord pad, percussive noise layer, and spatialized source. Render six versions. A is an object-only control. B forces every event to answer a prior event at beat, phrase, or section scale, including silence as an answer [S1]. C moves the chord pad only by adjacent steps in a small Tonnetz-like graph while keeping the cadence fixed [S5]. D uses nearest-accessible transitions: smallest voice-leading, spectral-density, or rhythmic-subdivision changes, echoing metastable path dependence [S2]. E varies only symbolic/acoustic alignment by offsetting envelope peaks and room tails by 80–160 ms, testing prosodic instability from unit mismatch [S3]. F preserves pitch contour and phrase identity while adapting noise, reverb clarity, transient softness, and stereo position, borrowing the invariant/adaptive split from enhancement models and spatial relation logic [S4, S6]. A disconfirming result would be that blind listeners cannot identify perceptual differences beyond loudness or timbre.

parameters.value: six fixed objects, six relation-only variations
alignment offsets of 80 ms and 160 ms
three relation scales: beat, phrase, section

dawChecklist: Create six audio/MIDI objects and freeze or bounce them so object identity stays fixed across versions.
Render Version A as an intuitive object-only control.
Render Version B by assigning every object entry a call/answer target at beat, phrase, or section scale; include at least two silent answers.
Render Version C by routing the chord pad through a short adjacency-only harmonic graph while keeping the final cadence identical to A.
Render Version D by replacing leaps with nearest-accessible changes in voice leading, density, and subdivision; reserve one deliberate high-pressure leap.
Render Version E twice with identical notes but envelope/room-tail offsets of 80 ms and 160 ms.
Render Version F with pitch/rhythm identity preserved but reverb clarity, noise, transient softness, and stereo position adapted over time.
Blind-label the renders and rate dialogue, spatial coherence, stability, and inevitability from 1–7.

protocol.listeningContext: studio headphones, matched integrated loudness before rating
protocol.listeningMethod: blind A/B/X-style shuffle with 1–7 ratings for dialogue, spatial coherence, stability, and inevitability
whatVaries: adaptive surface mapping for noise/reverb/transients/spatial position
